about.title: Special Factoring and a Factoring Strategy
about.length_note: About 30 minutes: two special patterns plus a checklist is a full half-hour class if each is shown with an example and a check question. Note for the editor: web search was unavailable when this lesson was written, so no sources were read and none are cited. The math is standard. Please check the examples against an OpenStax algebra text before publishing.

say.text: Welcome to class 39. Today we learn two shortcut patterns for factoring, and then a checklist for any polynomial.

show.text: Special Factoring and a Factoring Strategy

say.text: First, a quick reminder. Factoring means rewriting a sum as a product. For example, x² + 5x + 6 becomes (x + 2)(x + 3).

show.text: Sum: x² + 5x + 6 | Product: (x + 2)(x + 3)

say.text: Pattern one starts with perfect squares. A perfect square is what you get when you multiply something by itself. 9 is one, because 3 × 3 = 9.
Variables can be squares too. x² is x times x. x⁴ is x² times x². And 25x² is (5x) times (5x).

show.text: x² = (x)(x) | x⁴ = (x²)(x²) | 25x² = (5x)(5x)

say.text: Now the first pattern: a difference of squares. That is one square minus another square, with exactly two terms, like x² − 49.

show.text: Difference of squares: a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b)

say.text: Why does it work? Multiply (a − b)(a + b) out. You get a² + ab − ab − b². The two middle terms cancel, so only a² − b² is left.

show.text: (a − b)(a + b) | = a² + ab − ab − b² | = a² − b²

say.text: Example: x² − 49. x² is x squared. 49 is 7 squared. So the answer is (x − 7)(x + 7). Check it: the middle terms cancel.

ask.why: x² is x squared and 81 is 9 squared. A difference of squares splits into one minus and one plus: (x − 9)(x + 9).

say.text: Sometimes the first term has a number in front. Take 25x² − 16. 25x² is (5x) squared, and 16 is 4 squared. So it is (5x − 4)(5x + 4).

ask.why: 49x² is (7x) squared and 4 is 2 squared. So it is (7x − 2)(7x + 2). Multiply it back to check: the middle terms cancel.

say.text: A warning. A sum of squares, like x² + 9, will not factor with whole numbers. Try (x + 3)(x + 3). The middle term does not cancel, and you get x² + 6x + 9.

show.text: x² + 9 does not factor (it is called prime)

ask.q: Which one of these can be factored using a difference of squares?
ask.why: The pattern needs a MINUS between two squares. x² − 25 = (x − 5)(x + 5). A plus sign between squares does not factor this way.

say.text: A neat use is mental math. 12² − 8² is (12 − 8)(12 + 8). That is 4 × 20, which is 80. You can check it: 144 − 64 is 80.
Pattern two: a perfect square trinomial. It is what you get when you square a two-term answer, like (x + 5)(x + 5), which we write as (x + 5)².

show.text: Perfect square trinomial = a binomial times itself

say.text: Multiply (a + b)² out. You get a² + 2ab + b². With a minus it is a² − 2ab + b². The middle term is twice the product of the two square roots.

show.text: a² + 2ab + b² = (a + b)² | a² − 2ab + b² = (a − b)²

say.text: How do you spot one? Three quick tests. The first term is a square. The last term is a square. The middle term is twice the product of the two roots.

show.text: 1. First term is a square | 2. Last term is a square | 3. Middle = 2 × (root × root)

say.text: Try x² + 10x + 25. x² is x squared. 25 is 5 squared. Twice x times 5 is 10x, which matches. So it is (x + 5)².

ask.q: Which one is a perfect square trinomial?
ask.why: 16 is 4 squared, and twice x times 4 is 8x. Only x² + 8x + 16 matches, and it equals (x + 4)². In the others the middle term is not 8x.

say.text: With a minus in the middle, the answer has a minus. Take 9x² − 12x + 4. The roots are 3x and 2. Twice 3x times 2 is 12x. So it is (3x − 2)².

ask.why: The roots are 2x and 5, and twice 2x times 5 is 20x. The middle term is negative, so the answer is (2x − 5)². The other choices give a different middle term.

say.text: Now a checklist, for when you do not know which tool to use. Always go in this order. Step one: take out the greatest common factor, the GCF.

show.text: The Factoring Checklist

say.text: Step two: count the terms. Two terms? Look for a difference of squares. Three terms? Try a perfect square trinomial, then x² + bx + c or ax² + bx + c. Four terms? Try grouping.

show.text: 1. Take out the GCF | 2. Count the terms: 2 → difference of squares | 3 → perfect square, then x² + bx + c or ax² + bx + c | 4 → grouping | 3. Look again: can any factor be factored more? | 4. Multiply back to check

ask.q: You want to factor 3x² − 75. What do you do first?
ask.right: Take out the GCF, which is 3
wrong: Use difference of squares right away
ask.why: 3x² is not a perfect square, so the pattern does not fit yet. Take out the 3 first and you get 3(x² − 25). Then x² − 25 is a difference of squares.

say.text: Example: 2x² − 50. The GCF is 2, so we get 2(x² − 25). Two terms, with a minus between squares. So the answer is 2(x − 5)(x + 5). Never drop the 2!

ask.q: Which answer is factored COMPLETELY for 2x² − 50?
ask.why: (2x − 10)(x + 5) multiplies back correctly, but 2x − 10 still has a common factor of 2. So it is not finished. Dropping the 2 or using a square gives a different polynomial.

say.text: Factoring completely means you keep going until no piece can be factored more. Take x⁴ − 81. x⁴ is (x²) squared, and 81 is 9 squared. So it is (x² − 9)(x² + 9).

show.text: x⁴ − 81 | = (x² − 9)(x² + 9) | x² − 9 is another difference of squares | = (x − 3)(x + 3)(x² + 9)

ask.why: x² − 9 can be split again into (x − 3)(x + 3). But x² + 9 is a sum of squares, so it stays. (x − 9)(x + 9) would give x² − 81, not x⁴ − 81.

say.text: One more with the full checklist: 3x² + 18x + 27. GCF first: 3(x² + 6x + 9). Three terms. 9 is 3 squared, and 2 × x × 3 is 6x. So it is 3(x + 3)².

ask.why: The GCF is 5, which gives 5(x² − 4x + 4). The trinomial is a perfect square: (x − 2)². The other correct-looking forms are not finished, or they have the wrong middle term.

say.text: Let us wrap up. A difference of squares has two terms and a minus. A perfect square trinomial has three terms and a matching middle. And always start with the GCF.

show.text: a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b) | a² ± 2ab + b² = (a ± b)² | GCF first, factor completely, multiply back to check

say.text: Factoring is a skill that grows with practice, so go at your own pace. Next class we move on to quadratic functions and their graphs.

show.text: Next: Quadratic Functions and Their Graphs

other_side.claim: A sum of squares such as x² + 9 cannot be factored.
other_side.other_view: This is true only when we use real-number (whole-number) factors, which is what Algebra 1 uses. In a later course with complex numbers, x² + 9 does factor as (x + 3i)(x − 3i).

other_side.claim: Perfect square trinomials should be learned as a separate pattern.
other_side.other_view: Some teachers skip this pattern. They factor every trinomial with the general methods from classes 37 and 38 and let the repeated factor show up on its own. The pattern is faster once you spot it, but it is not required.
